To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) upper-limb muscles are more active than lower-limb during normal daily activities; 2) the amplitude of muscle activation during bursts is greater in lower-limb muscles; 3) temporal association in activity between muscles is high for lower-limb muscles and relatively weak for upper-limb muscles; and 4) there is no association between the duration muscle activity in 24 h and the reported proportion of type I fibers.
10-h recordings of EMG activity of limb muscles revealed that upper-limb muscles are active more than lower-limb and that there are large differences in the amplitude of EMG bursts between muscles.

10-h EMG recordings in men and women show that upper-limb muscles are more active than lower-limb muscle and that there is a strong temporal association in the activity of muscles in lower limbs but not in upper limbs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
long-term muscle activity in humans, a factor that may be related to muscle fiber type.
the quantification of muscle activity in humans during normal daily use and with the relation between muscle activity and fiber-type composition.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proportion of type II muscle fibers in humans does not appear to be related to the duration of daily activity of limb muscles during normal use.
the activity of the upper-limb muscles is more frequent than that of the lower-limb muscles, but when leg muscles are active they are activated more forcefully than arm muscles.

, although the duration of muscle activity is not associated with the percentage of type I fibers, the intensity of activity (as measured by the amplitude of the EMG signal) is associated with the percentage and cross-sectional area of type I fibers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in humans, there is no association between the proportion of type 1 fibers and the duration of muscle activity during long-term recordings.
the upper-limb muscles are more active than the lower-limb muscles and the duration of muscle activity is not related to the percentage of type I muscle fiber in men and women.
, on average, men and women spend more time activating their hand and arm muscles than their leg muscles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the duration of activity of limb muscles of healthy men and women is different and does not correlate with the reported fiber type proportions.
, in humans, the duration of muscle activity is not a good predictor of the proportion of type 1 fibers in the muscles.
the activity of muscles in humans is highly variable and that there is no clear association between muscle activity and fiber type.
